blocks.text: Ns. [=Neo-Syriac]: also ܦܣܬܩܐ [פסתקא] PSm. [=Payne Smith, Thesaurus syriacus] 3199. 3838. Maclean [=Maclean, Dictionary of Vernacular Syriac] sv. [=sub voce]: a nut, probably imprecise for a pistachio nut. From Malula, Bergsträsser [=Bergsträsser, Neuaramäische Märchen; Glossar] records 93_{19}, Glossar [=Bergsträsser, Glossar des neuaramäischen Dialekts von Maʿlūla] 27: fuscḳō. A terrain covered with pistachios east of Malūlā: ṣaḥrṯa 85. Foreign-language forms: on Gn. [=Genesis] 43, 11, Raši [=Rashi, commentary] cites for boṭnīm the explanation of R. [=Rabbi] Machir: פשטציאם ed. [=edition] Berliner [=Berliner, Raschi: Commentar zum Pentateuch], פישטקיאם Bible ed. Basel 1620. Rashi states that he does not know what bŏṭnīm are, but that he found the explanation pistazias in R. Machir. This, however, he evidently does not know, and he connects it with the word aparsĕḳīn, peach. Ibn Esra [=Abraham Ibn Ezra, commentary] likewise knows nothing of pistachios. He says that some take boṭnīm to be walnuts. RDK. [=Rabbi David Kimhi, Sefer ha-Shorashim]: pignola, according to others: fustuḳ. פיניוניש Epstein, Miḳadm. [=Epstein, Miḳadmonijjōt ha-jĕhūdīm] 126 = boṭnīm. Nocili, avellana: Bacher, Prüfstein d. Men. b. Salomo [=Bacher, Der Prüfstein des Menachem ben Salomo], p. [=page] 3 n. [=note] = boṭnīm. Sechel tōb [=Sekhel Tov, ed. Buber], p. 11: boṭnīm is the resin of the tree boṭna: the tree = לרזו, the resin = טרגנטו. In Mb. [=?] 31 boṭnīm is rendered by פיטולש (l. [=read] pignolas).

Tanner's sumac — widespread throughout the whole Mediterranean region — is called in Mishnaic Hebrew אוג Flora [=Löw, Die Flora der Juden] 3, 219. The word is also used in modern Eretz-Yisrael Hebrew (Hasade [=Hasade, Hebrew agricultural monthly] 3, 233. 4, 391). It is a tree (Pea [=Mishnah Peah] 1, 5. Sifra [=Sifra, midrash on Leviticus] 87^{b}), whose ripening berries turn reddish (Maas. [=tractate Maʿaserot] 1, 2). On this basis Jastrow [=Jastrow, Dictionary of the Targum, the Talmud etc.] wrongly emends האיבין ארומים, LA. [=variant reading] האובים, האיבום (ms. [=manuscript] in Zuckermandel, Errata [=Zuckermandel, Tosefta, errata]) T. [=Tosefta, ed. Zuckermandel] Maas. r. [=tractate Maʿaser rishon] 1, 81_{18} to האוגין, for it is the bh. [=Biblical Hebrew] אב (Schwarz, Tosifta [=Schwarz, Tosefta] 1, 317).

The tree was less esteemed in Judaea than in the rest of Eretz Yisrael (Dem. [=tractate Demai] 1, 1), where it grows everywhere today. Luncz [=Kaftor waferaḥ, ed. Luncz] asserts that it grows especially in the region of Hebron (Kaftor [=Estori ha-Farḥi, Kaftor waferaḥ] 482). On the Carmel it is rarer (ZDPV. [=Zeitschrift des Deutschen Palästina-Vereins] 30, 134), yet a ruin there is called chirbet summāḳa (a. O. [=at the place cited] 158). The leaves still serve today for the preparation of tanbark (H. Fischer, Wirtschaftsgeogr. von Syrien [=Fischer, Wirtschaftsgeographie von Syrien] 74).

The young leaves,*) as well as the fruit and bark (P. [=Post, Flora of Syria, Palestine and Sinai] 206), were already used in antiquity for dyeing and tanning (Kel. [=tractate Kelim] 26, 3) (עלי האוג TŠvi [=Tosefta Shevi'it, ed. Zuckermandel] 5, 68_{6}; imprecisely j [=Jerusalem Talmud, ed. Krotoschin] 7, 37^{b}_{15} the root, which incidentally also dyes yellow. Ratner [=Ratner, Ahawath Zion wīrūšalajim] z. St. [=on the passage] S. [=page] 62, Z. [=line] 3 v. u. [=from below]. Herschberg, Haëreg [=Herschberg, Hāereg we-taăsijjat hāereg] 261). The identification with the arab. [=Arabic] sumaḳ in Aruch [=Aruch, ed. Kohut] and Maimūnī [=Maimonides, commentary on the Mishnah] (Natan [=?], WB. [=dictionary] 10. 24), also Kaftor 482. 527; yet cornelian cherry has repeatedly been substituted for it (R. Gēršōm [=Rabbenu Gershom] REJ. [=Revue des Etudes Juives] 7, 66 cornouiller,
Hence ns. ʿallja (= leaf) tanner's sumac (Malula-Gl. [=Bergsträsser, Glossar des neuaramäischen Dialekts von Maʿlūla] 3).
